cards.text: Some time later, two officers offend their master, Pharaoh, the king of Egypt: his chief cupbearer and his chief baker. Pharaoh is angry with them both, and friend, a BAKER in trouble with the boss has me sweating under this hat.

cards.question: Pharaoh locks up his chief cupbearer and chief baker in the same prison where Joseph is confined.
In the prison, the captain of the guard assigns the cupbearer and the baker a personal attendant. Who is it?

cards.text: After they've been in custody for some time, both men have a dream on the same night, and each dream has its own meaning. Friend, in all my years in that junk drawer, my wildest night was one of the dead batteries rolling over.
The next morning, Joseph comes in to see them. He takes one look at those two.

cards.question: When Joseph comes to the cupbearer and the baker in the morning, he sees that they are ___.

cards.text: So Joseph asks them, “Why are your faces so downcast today?” He's locked up himself and he's STILL checking on everybody else, and friend, I know that move, because I did it for every scared newcomer who slid into my drawer.

cards.question: Joseph asks the cupbearer and the baker why their faces are so downcast. What do they tell him?

answers.text: We had dreams and no one can interpret them
The guards here have been cruel to us
We have no way to send word home

cards.question: Joseph answers them, “Don’t interpretations belong to ___? Tell me your dreams.”

cards.text: The chief cupbearer goes first. In his dream there's a vine in front of him with three branches, and as it buds, the blossoms open and the clusters ripen into grapes.

cards.question: In the cupbearer's dream, the grapes are ripe and Pharaoh's cup is in his hand. What does he do next?

answers.text: Squeezes the grapes into it for Pharaoh
Pours the cup out on the ground

cards.text: Joseph replies, “This is the interpretation: The three branches are three days.” Friend, you hand ME a dream and I need a week, two batches and a nap.

cards.question: The three branches are three days. What does Joseph say Pharaoh will do for the cupbearer within three days?

answers.text: Release him to go back home
Put him in charge of the prison

cards.text: Then Joseph asks for something. When it goes well for the cupbearer, please remember Joseph, show him kindness and mention him to Pharaoh, so Pharaoh might bring him out of this prison.

cards.question: Joseph tells the cupbearer he did something to deserve being put in this dungeon.

cards.text: When the chief baker sees that the cupbearer's interpretation was favorable, he speaks up: he had a dream too. Fellow baker, I get it, I'd have been first in line.

cards.question: The cupbearer's vine had three branches. How many baskets are on the chief baker's head in his dream?

cards.text: Baskets of white bread stacked on his head, and the top one holds all sorts of baked goods for Pharaoh. My hat's tall, friend, but even it has limits.

cards.question: In the chief baker's dream, something is happening to Pharaoh's baked goods in the top basket. What is it?

answers.text: Birds are eating them out of the basket
They are tumbling down to the ground
Servants are carrying them all away

cards.text: Joseph replies with that line again: “This is the interpretation: The three baskets are three days.” Friend, birds eating out of the basket on your head? I don't love where this is going.

cards.question: Joseph tells the chief baker that Pharaoh will restore him to his position, just like the cupbearer.

cards.text: For the cupbearer, Joseph said Pharaoh would lift up his head. For the baker, Pharaoh will lift off his head and hang him on a tree, and the birds will eat his flesh.
On the third day, Pharaoh holds a feast for all his officials. I bet two men in that prison were counting every hour.

cards.question: On the third day, Pharaoh holds a feast for all his officials. What's the occasion?

cards.text: And right there, in front of all his officials, Pharaoh lifts up the heads of the chief cupbearer and the chief baker.

cards.question: Pharaoh restores the chief cupbearer to his position, so he once again places the ___ in Pharaoh's hand.
Pharaoh spares the chief baker too.
Joseph asked the chief cupbearer to remember him and mention him to Pharaoh. Now the cupbearer is back serving Pharaoh. What does he do about Joseph?

answers.text: He sends for Joseph right away

cards.text: Forgotten. Friend, I know that one from the back of a junk drawer. We'll stop here for now, but trust me, this story is NOT done.

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 9 quotes "Don't interpretations belong to ___? Tell me your dreams.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: The passage picks up in the middle of Joseph's story (passage 3 of 14), but the opening card never mentions Joseph or that he is already in prison. The first time the baker learns where Joseph is comes from the wording of the card 2 question.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on. If the passage starts in the middle of a thought, it gives the context.

findings.problem: The joke does not match the core action. The fact is two men having meaningful dreams on the same night, and the comparison is a dead battery rolling over. That is a different action, it doesn't click right away, and it reads more like a strained callback than a laugh.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: "Egypt" is a place, while "God" and "Pharaoh" are persons who could hold interpretations. Because it is a different kind of answer, it is easy to rule out.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The joke 'I'd have been first in line' contradicts the moment. The chief baker speaks second, and only after he sees that the cupbearer's interpretation was favorable (Gen 40:16). The comparison does not share the core action of waiting to see how it goes first.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The setup line 'I don't love where this is going' signals bad news right before the true/false card asking whether the baker will be restored like the cupbearer. It rules out the answer 'True' and gives away card 6.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The closing line 'trust me, this story is NOT done' copies the doc's example line ('Trust me, friend, this story's not done') almost word for word instead of being a new line.

rule.text: The examples show the idea. Write your own line each time.
